title: Thermal imaging: specifications, interpretation and household uses
tldr: Thermal cameras display infrared contrast, not a guaranteed identification or a view through walls. Compare the actual sensor, sensitivity and intended task, then verify any important finding by an appropriate independent method.
steps: Distinguish outdoor observation from building inspection or calibrated temperature measurement. These require different capabilities.
Check native thermal sensor resolution, field of view, sensitivity and whether the device supports temperature measurement.
Ordinary glass, reflective surfaces, weather and obstructions affect interpretation. A bright patch alone does not identify its cause.
Use qualified help for electrical, structural or medical concerns. Do not open hazardous equipment to investigate an interesting image.

sections.heading: A thermal image is an interpretation of radiation

blocks.text: A thermal camera forms an image from infrared radiation and translates differences into a display. A coloured palette is a visual convention rather than the scene’s visible colour. Some imagers also provide calibrated temperature estimates; others are intended chiefly for observation. Establish which kind of device you have before interpreting a number on the screen as a meaningful measurement.

For a household inspection, separate the observation from its proposed cause. A cool-looking patch on a wall could have several explanations, including a temperature difference or reflection. Record the surface, weather, indoor heating or cooling conditions and a normal photograph. Repeated observations under comparable conditions make a better inspection record than one dramatic palette image.

references: FLIR OEM · Choosing a thermal imager

sections.heading: Specifications that deserve a place on the comparison sheet

blocks.caption: Compare the underlying capability
rows: Native sensor resolution
The thermal detector’s pixel grid.
Is the advertised number the sensor or only the screen?
Field of view
The scene width and height visible through the lens.
Does it fit the intended observation or inspection task?
Thermal sensitivity / NETD
The ability to distinguish small thermal differences under stated conditions.
Under what test conditions was the value specified?
Temperature measurement
Whether the system estimates temperature, rather than only displaying contrast.
What calibration, limits and settings apply?
Focus and operating limits
How and where the device can produce a usable image.
What conditions does the manual actually permit?

blocks.text: Thermal sensitivity and spatial resolution answer different questions. More detector pixels do not by themselves establish sensitivity, accurate temperature measurement or a useful lens for your task. Compare manufacturers’ datasheets rather than collecting the largest number in each advertisement. Keep incompatible test conditions visible instead of treating unlike specifications as a fair ranking.

blocks.caption: Interpretation terms worth knowing
rows: NETD / thermal sensitivity
The ability to distinguish small thermal differences under stated test conditions; lower reported values can indicate better sensitivity when tests are comparable.
Emissivity
How effectively a surface emits infrared radiation; shiny low-emissivity surfaces can make reflections especially important.
Radiometric image
A file that retains measurement information, where supported; a screenshot of a color palette may not retain it.
Automatic gain / palette
Display choices that change contrast and colors; two differently scaled images may look different without a matching physical change.
Focus and field of view
Determine which surface detail is resolved and how much of the surrounding scene appears.

references: FLIR OEM · Choosing a thermal imager

sections.heading: What glass, walls and reflections change

blocks.text: Ordinary thermal imaging does not provide a movie-style view through walls. A wall’s surface pattern may change because of conditions within the building, but that is a surface observation rather than direct sight of what is behind it. Ordinary window glass also prevents the expected view through the window for typical long-wave thermal cameras; reflections can dominate the image. Shiny surfaces create similar interpretation problems.

blocks.caption: Common interpretation traps
rows: A bright patch on glass
Assuming it is an object beyond the window.
Consider reflection and use an appropriate ordinary view.
A pattern on a wall
Assuming it identifies a hidden fault.
Record conditions and seek a suitable building assessment.
A shiny metal surface
Treating apparent temperature as unquestionable.
Check measurement limitations and manufacturer guidance.
A partially hidden object
Assuming missing detail proves nothing is present.
Retain uncertainty and use another safe source of information.

blocks.text: Do not open electrical panels, climb onto a damaged roof or enter a compromised structure just to chase a thermal pattern. An image can support a question for a qualified provider; it does not remove the hazard involved in obtaining an answer.

references: FLIR · Walls, glass and infrared limitations

sections.heading: Weather and the difference between detection and identification

blocks.text: Rain and fog can reduce thermal viewing performance. The amount depends on atmospheric conditions and equipment; thermal imaging is not an all-weather guarantee. An outdoor image also depends on whether the subject contrasts sufficiently with its surroundings. Treat any advertised distance as a claim tied to a test and a specific observation task, not as a promise of clear identification in every scene.

Detection means noticing something in the image. Recognition or identification requires enough reliable detail to determine what it is. For a civilian wildlife observation, a shape that might be an animal is still uncertain until appropriate detail or another safe observation establishes it. Never approach a hazard or act against a person because an ambiguous thermal shape appears on a screen.

items: Record weather and surroundings during a demonstration.
Compare a live image, not only an edited promotional clip.
Describe which detail was actually visible.
Keep uncertainty when objects overlap, contrast is weak or the scene is obstructed.

sections.heading: Household inspection: use the image to ask a better question

blocks.text: A practical, low-risk inspection record contains the room or area, date, normal visible photograph where appropriate, thermal image, relevant conditions and the question for a qualified professional. For example, a repeated unusual surface pattern near a window can be recorded as “please assess this area,” rather than declared a leak from the image alone. Include changes in weather, heating or cooling that could affect comparison.

blocks.caption: A responsible inspection workflow
items: From an ordinary safe position, record the pattern.
Write the conditions and the uncertainty.
Ask the appropriate qualified provider about the actual concern.
Use the inspection or another suitable method before choosing a repair.
blocks.note: An educational decision aid, not equipment certification or a live assessment.

blocks.text: Do not use a consumer camera as a replacement for carbon monoxide alarms, smoke alarms, electrical inspection or medical assessment. It is not a reason to stay in a building during a fire or gas concern. During a disaster, damaged structures and contaminated areas remain hazardous even if the image looks ordinary. The correct first action is protective distance and appropriate help, not collecting a better picture.
If using images for a landlord or contractor, keep the original files and describe them plainly. Avoid implying specialist certification that neither the operator nor the equipment provides.

sections.heading: Power, records and a sensible purchase decision

blocks.text: Before purchase, decide how often the device will be used, whether it needs a phone, and what still works without an app account or network. Check battery arrangements, permitted environmental conditions, warranty support and availability of service. A specialised inspection camera and an observation monocular may both be called thermal but provide very different interfaces and capabilities. Select for the actual task.

items: Write one primary civilian use and a realistic frequency of use.
Compare native sensor data separately from display resolution.
Ask for sample files and a live demonstration for the intended task.
Check recording, wireless features and personal-data handling.
Include protection, service and any training in the total budget.

blocks.text: Store images privately when they show a home’s layout or household activity. Set a maintenance reminder and keep the manual with the equipment record. For an occasional household question, hiring a qualified inspection service may make more sense than purchasing a device and trying to interpret an unfamiliar image. For an established observation hobby, a carefully defined trial can show whether the device adds value.

Return to basic preparedness priorities if the purchase would consume the money needed for water, medicines, safe temperature, communication or transport. Advanced technology is most useful when it supports a clear plan and an appropriate verification process. It should not create confidence beyond what the image actually establishes.

sections.heading: Spatial detail, field of view and digital zoom

blocks.text: Native detector resolution counts the thermal samples across and down the sensor. Field of view describes how much scene those samples cover. Read them together: an equal pixel grid covering a wider scene assigns each sample a larger share of that scene. The lens, focus and imaging conditions still determine which detail is actually resolved.

blocks.caption: An invented same-view sampling comparison
rows: The number of samples in this illustrative grid.
Twice as many samples along each axis and four times as many overall.
Enlarged 160 × 120 output
Still 19,200 original detector samples
More output pixels do not imply more independently captured thermal information.

blocks.text: The example assumes the same field of view and discusses sampling only. It does not establish identification distance, temperature accuracy, lens quality or superiority under different weather. A high-resolution display can make the view comfortable without changing the thermal information captured by a lower-resolution detector.

Digital zoom crops or enlarges the existing view. Interpolated output estimates extra display values; it does not measure new points in the scene. A narrow view may show a smaller part of an inspection area at once, while a wider view supplies more context. For a household inspection, note which actual surface the image includes rather than interpreting an enlarged patch as a complete view of the area.

Compare native detector pixels, field of view, focus range and exported-image dimensions in separate columns. Reject a comparison that silently changes one of those conditions. A camera should be selected for a defined observation or inspection question, with an independent method for conclusions that affect safety.

references: FLIR OEM · Choosing a thermal imager

sections.heading: Sensitivity, measurement accuracy and palette contrast

blocks.text: NETD describes thermal sensitivity under stated test conditions. Absolute temperature accuracy answers a different question: how close a supported measurement is to the actual surface temperature within its specified uncertainty. A camera can resolve small differences while still needing calibration and correct interpretation for reliable temperature values.

blocks.caption: Keep three claims separate
rows: Sensitivity / NETD
Ability to distinguish small thermal differences under the stated test.
Absolute temperature accuracy or a universal detection range.
Measurement accuracy
The specified uncertainty of a supported temperature estimate under defined conditions.
A correct estimate on every material without appropriate settings or interpretation.
Displayed contrast
How the image's range is mapped to shades or colours.
A corresponding difference in physical severity.

blocks.text: As an invented unit example, 50 mK is a temperature difference of 0.05 °C. That sensitivity figure would not mean an absolute temperature measurement is accurate to ±0.05 °C. Compare the separate accuracy statement and its conditions if measurement matters. An observation-only device may provide useful contrast without supporting calibrated temperature measurement at all.

A palette is a display convention. If two images use different displayed ranges, a small physical difference can occupy a large part of one palette and a small part of the other. Read the scale and conditions before comparing colours. A dramatic red area is not automatically hotter than every red area in another image.

Surface emission and reflection further affect interpretation. FLIR illustrates polished metal reflecting surrounding thermal radiation; an apparent warm area can therefore reflect another heat source. Record the surface and conditions and use qualified thermography or building assessment when the consequence matters. Do not treat colour, a single pixel or a consumer measurement as an electrical, structural or medical diagnosis.

without_help: If a pattern has no clear explanation, keep the original image and record the conditions rather than assigning it a cause. Use ordinary visible inspection where safe; obtain appropriate assessment for electrical, structural or moisture concerns.
household: Keep visible and thermal photographs together, label the location and date, and store records privately. Make batteries, lens protection and the correct manual available to the person who uses the camera.
pack_now: Model, native sensor resolution, measurement capability, battery requirements, manual, care limits and an inspection-log template.
next: Compare live images under the same conditions. Check field of view, native resolution, thermal sensitivity, focus and whether original measurement files can be exported.
watch: A hot-looking patch may be a reflection, and an observation imager may not measure temperature. Do not use a consumer camera to replace alarms or open hazardous equipment to investigate an image.

intro_note: Thermal contrast, scene detail and temperature measurement are separate capabilities. A thermal image shows radiation from visible surfaces; it is not a view through ordinary walls.
